title: Predictivism as a Scope Ambiguity: De Re and De Dicto Confirmation of Searched Hypotheses
thesis: When a hypothesis H is selected from a large space for its fit to E, E confirms H (de re) exactly as much as it would have if H had been proposed in advance. What E confirms less is the de dicto proposition 'the output of search S is true'. The Bayesian denial of predictivism and the error-statistical affirmation of it are both correct, about different propositions.
argument_sketch: Distinguish two objects of evaluation: the hypothesis picked out rigidly, and the hypothesis picked out under the description 'whatever S returns on E'. For a coherent agent, P(H|E) is fixed by the prior and likelihood of H and does not depend on how H was found. P(the S-winner is true | E), however, must average over all the hypotheses S could have returned, so it is discounted by the search's reach. I then argue that scientific acceptance, reporting, and policy reliance usually take the de dicto object, because what gets endorsed is the method's verdict. On this reading the physicist's distinction between local and global significance (the look-elsewhere effect) is the same scope distinction. Most canonical predictivist cases have a true de dicto reading and a false de re reading.
why_new: White (2003), Hitchcock and Sober (2004), and Howson and Urbach each locate the predictive advantage in one place: the predictor's reliability, overfitting, or nowhere. None of them notices that the competing verdicts attach to different propositions. Treating the debate as a scope ambiguity explains why both camps' intuitions are stable, and it gives a principled account of when timing-based judgments are apt.

objection.objection:
The de dicto discount disappears once the agent conditions on her total evidence, so the scope distinction cannot do the reconciling work. After the search has run, the agent knows E and knows that S returned H on E. Given that knowledge, 'the output of S is true' and 'H is true' are equivalent. So P(the S-winner is true | E, S returned H) = P(H | E), and the two objects of evaluation have the same posterior.

The author's discounted quantity comes from 'averaging over all the hypotheses S could have returned.' That average is over counterfactual data and counterfactual outputs. It is a pre-data or unconditional reliability of the procedure, not a credence in a proposition given E. What the thesis calls a scope distinction is really the familiar contrast between a conditional probability and an unconditional error rate. That contrast is the Bayesian/error-statistical dispute itself, restated, not something that dissolves it (Howson and Urbach 2006; Mayo 1996, 2018).

The look-elsewhere effect does not fit the proposed mapping either. In Bayesian analyses of searches such as the Higgs mass scan, the trials factor reappears as prior dilution over the search range, the Occam factor in the Bayes factor. That penalty attaches to the rigidly designated hypothesis 'there is a resonance at m₀,' which is the de re object. So either the search's reach is already in the prior, and the de re posterior is penalized too, contradicting the first half of the thesis. Or the global p-value is a frequentist procedure property that has no de dicto credal counterpart. Either way, local versus global significance is not the de re/de dicto distinction (cf. Gross and Vitells 2010).

Finally, the reconciliation misstates the error statistician's position. Mayo's severity claim is that H itself, de re, has passed a test with low probative capacity. Telling her she is 'correct about a different proposition' assigns her a view she explicitly rejects.
objection.rationale:
The paper's novelty lies entirely in the second half: a de dicto proposition whose confirmation is discounted while de re confirmation is not. The de re half is just standard Bayesian anti-predictivism. If the de dicto posterior collapses into the de re posterior under conditionalization on total evidence, the paper has no distinctive positive claim. The look-elsewhere identification, which is the most interesting application, would also be false as stated.

This is not quite fatal. The author could retreat to the claim that acceptance, reporting, and policy are properly governed by unconditional procedure reliability rather than by posterior credence. That is a substantive normative thesis about which quantity should guide endorsement. But it is a different paper, a defense of a reliabilist or error-statistical norm of acceptance. It would have to argue for that norm against Bayesian decision theory rather than present the dispute as a misunderstanding about scope.

A second escape is to model agents who cannot tractably conditionalize on S's output, making the de dicto quantity a credence for bounded agents. That would need serious development, for example via the old-evidence and logical-omniscience literature (Garber 1983; Hacking 1967). Without one of these moves the central reconciliation fails.

closest_work.work: Maher, P. (1988) 'Prediction, accommodation, and the logic of discovery', PSA 1988 vol. 1; Maher (1990) 'How prediction enhances confirmation', in Dunn & Gupta (eds.), Truth or Consequences
closest_work.relation: The canonical Bayesian predictivism. Successful prediction is evidence that the predictor's *method* is reliable, and only derivatively evidence for the hypothesis. Your de dicto object, 'what S returns is true', is close to Maher's method-reliability proposition. Your de re / de dicto vocabulary relabels his split between the theory and the method that produced it.

closest_work.work: Kahn, J., Landsburg, S. & Stockman, A. (1992) 'On novel confirmation', BJPS 43: 503-516
closest_work.relation: Gives a formal Bayesian model in which novel success raises credence in the scientist or method rather than in the hypothesis as such. Its pattern matches your diagnosis: the hypothesis-level posterior is fixed, and the advantage lives at the level of the generating process.

closest_work.work: White, R. (2003) 'The epistemic advantage of prediction over accommodation', Mind 112: 653-683
closest_work.relation: Locates the predictive advantage in what the prediction reveals about whether the theorist is tracking the truth. White's account is again an advantage attached to the process rather than to the rigidly designated hypothesis. Your thesis needs to say what it adds beyond recasting White's mechanism as a scope distinction.

closest_work.work: Barnes, E. C. (2008) The Paradox of Predictivism, Cambridge UP
closest_work.relation: Distinguishes 'thin' and 'tempered' predictivism and defends the view that prediction confirms via endorsers and their background beliefs. Barnes explicitly frames the debate as a question of which proposition is being confirmed. That framing is the core of your reconciliation.

closest_work.work: Hitchcock, C. & Sober, E. (2004) 'Prediction versus accommodation and the risk of overfitting', BJPS 55: 1-34
closest_work.relation: Recasts predictivism in terms of the estimated predictive accuracy of the *procedure* (Akaike-style) versus support for a fixed hypothesis. This is a direct precedent for the claim that the predictivist and anti-predictivist answer different questions.

closest_work.work: Mayo, D. (1996) Error and the Growth of Experimental Knowledge, chs. 8-9; Mayo (2018) Statistical Inference as Severe Testing, incl. the Higgs/look-elsewhere excursions
closest_work.relation: Mayo argues at length that the likelihood principle makes selection effects ('hunting', 'data-dredging', use-novelty violations) invisible to Bayesian posteriors, while severity, being a property of the testing procedure, registers them. She discusses the LEE explicitly. Her diagnosis of the Bayesian/error-statistical disagreement is essentially yours. She does not concede that both sides are right, but you need to engage her reasons for refusing that concession.

closest_work.work: Staley, K. (1996) 'Novelty, severity, and history in the testing of hypotheses: the case of the top quark', Phil. Sci. 63 (Proc.): S248-S255; Dawid, R. (2017) 'Bayesian perspectives on the discovery of the Higgs particle', Synthese; Cousins, R. (2017) 'The Jeffreys-Lindley paradox and discovery criteria in high energy physics', Synthese
closest_work.relation: These papers already connect tuning, selection, and the look-elsewhere effect in HEP to the prediction/accommodation debate and to Bayesian versus frequentist accounts. Cousins and Dawid show how a Bayesian recovers a trials-factor-like penalty through prior dilution over the search range. That is a *de re* mechanism, and it threatens your identification of the LEE with a scope distinction.

closest_work.work: Scott, J. & Berger, J. (2010) 'Bayes and empirical-Bayes multiplicity adjustment in the variable-selection problem', Annals of Statistics 38: 2587-2619
closest_work.relation: This is the standard statistical treatment of how multiplicity enters a Bayesian analysis: through the prior over the hypothesis space, not through a separate de dicto object. Your account must explain why this is not the right reading of the canonical cases.

novelty.note:
The substance is largely anticipated. The claim that P(H|E) is insensitive to discovery history while prediction confirms something about the method or predictor is the Maher / Kahn-Landsburg-Stockman / White / Barnes line. The claim that error statistics registers selection effects because it evaluates procedures is Mayo's. The reconciliation 'each side is right about a different object' is already explicit in Hitchcock & Sober and implicit in Barnes. What may be new is the de re / de dicto packaging (I know of no paper that uses that apparatus for this purpose, though I cannot rule one out) and the strong claim that scientific acceptance takes the de dicto object.

The argument as sketched has a serious technical gap. For an agent who conditions on E and knows S, the description 'the S-winner on E' picks out H with probability 1. So P(the S-winner is true | E) = P(H | E). The de dicto proposition collapses into the de re one once E is fully conditioned on. Your 'averaging over all the hypotheses S could have returned' is not a posterior on E. It is either (a) a pre-data, unconditional error rate of the procedure, or (b) a posterior on a coarsening of E, such as 'S returned some hypothesis with fit above t'. Your scope distinction is therefore really the old conditional-versus-unconditional divide (cf. Berger & Wolpert, The Likelihood Principle; Kiefer's conditional confidence). That divide is exactly what separates Bayesians from error statisticians. If so, the thesis does not reconcile the two camps. It restates their disagreement as a choice of evaluand, and you must then argue that the coarsened or unconditional object is the right target for acceptance and reporting. Mayo argues for that; Bayesians deny it.

The LEE identification is also contestable. In HEP the trials factor can be reproduced, approximately, by a Bayesian prior spread over the mass range, so no de dicto object is needed. You must show the canonical predictivist cases are not better handled this way.

To claim novelty, you should (1) state precisely which coarsening of E the de dicto posterior conditions on and defend that choice, (2) answer Mayo directly, and (3) show your account classifies some cases differently from Maher, White, and Barnes.

title: Graded Predictivism: Measuring Accommodation in Bits of Leakage
thesis: How far a fit's confirmatory force should be discounted for accommodation is bounded by the mutual information between the data and the choice of hypothesis. 'Prediction' is the special case where that information is zero. Timing matters only as a crude upper bound on this leakage.
argument_sketch: Results in adaptive data analysis (Russo and Zou; Dwork et al.) bound the bias of a data-selected statistic by I(E; choice of H). I adapt these bounds to the evidential setting and show that the excess apparent support of a selected hypothesis over its honest support is controlled by this quantity. The prediction/accommodation dichotomy therefore conceals a continuum. Examples on the continuum include hypotheses chosen after seeing a noisy summary of the data, a coarse histogram, or one variable among many, and each warrants intermediate confirmation. Timing is neither necessary nor sufficient for zero leakage: post-data choices made blind to the data have none, and pre-data choices informed by correlated pilot data have some.
why_new: The philosophical literature treats novelty as binary, whether temporal (Popper, Lakatos), heuristic (Zahar, Worrall), or use-based. The information-theoretic results in computer science have not been brought into confirmation theory. This thesis supplies a quantitative, graded replacement for use-novelty and makes Worrall's criterion a limiting case.

objection.objection: The argument moves from a property of selection procedures to a claim about the confirmation of a particular hypothesis, and that move does not go through. The Russo–Zou and Dwork et al. bounds have the form |E[φ_T − μ_T]| ≤ σ√(2 I(T; data)). This is a bound on expected bias, averaged over the joint distribution of datasets and the choices a fixed selection rule would make on them. I(E; choice of H) is therefore not a feature of the actual episode, in which this E was observed and this H was proposed. It is a feature of a counterfactual policy: what the scientist would have chosen had the data come out otherwise. Confirmation, on any standard account (Bayesian, likelihoodist, or Hempelian), is a relation between the actual E and the actual H. Three problems follow. (i) Indeterminacy: a scientist who looks at the data and proposes H usually has no well-defined selection rule over alternative datasets. The value of I depends on how that counterfactual policy is specified, so the advertised continuum inherits a reference-class problem. Your own examples (blind post-data choice, pilot-informed pre-data choice) get their verdicts only because the procedure is stipulated, not because anything about the evidence fixes it. (ii) Expectation versus single case: a small average I is compatible with large realized leakage in the actual case (high pointwise mutual information on this dataset), and a large I is compatible with negligible leakage here. A bound on expected bias therefore cannot bound the discount owed to the fit actually in hand. To get a single-case bound you would need high-probability or pointwise results, such as the max-information bounds in Dwork et al. 2015, 'Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse'. Those bounds are not mutual-information bounds, so the thesis as stated would not survive the substitution. (iii) The quantity being bounded is not confirmation. The 'excess apparent support' that selection inflates is excess only relative to an unconditioned, frequentist measure of fit. Under a Bayesian treatment, data-dependent selection of which hypothesis to report is ignorable whenever the prior over hypotheses is fixed in advance and the selection depends only on the data (Dawid 1994, 'Selection paradoxes of Bayesian inference'). The posterior for the selected H is then exactly as it should be, and nothing needs discounting. So either the thesis assumes procedure-relative confirmation, which begs the question against the likelihood principle (Royall 1997; Howson & Urbach) and needs defending, or it is a thesis about error rates of procedures. In the second case it is a refinement of Mayo's severity framework, not a result about confirmation. Neither option delivers the advertised claim that the prediction/accommodation distinction in confirmation theory conceals an information-theoretic continuum.
objection.rationale: This objection targets the bridge principle the whole paper rests on: that a bound on the expected bias of a data-selected statistic is a bound on how much the confirmatory force of a particular fit should be discounted. If the objection goes unanswered, the formal results stay true but say nothing about confirmation. They become results about the reliability of policies, and the dissolution of the prediction/accommodation debate (White 2003; Lipton; Hitchcock & Sober 2004) does not follow. The claims about timing also lose their force, because they rely on I being determinate for actual cases. I rate it 4 rather than 5 because the author has a recoverable position. They can openly adopt an error-statistical or procedure-relative conception of support, argue that confirmation of a reported hypothesis is properly relative to the process that generated the report, and replace the mutual-information bounds with max-information or pointwise bounds that apply to single cases. That is a substantial rewrite with a narrower conclusion, but it is not an abandonment of the project.

closest_work.work: Russo, D. & Zou, J. (2016, AISTATS; expanded 2020, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory), 'Controlling Bias in Adaptive Data Analysis Using Information Theory' / 'How much does your data exploration overfit?'
closest_work.relation: Proves the core inequality: the bias of a data-selected statistic is bounded by sqrt(2σ²·I(X;T)). Its examples already include noisy selection, coarsened selection, and selection among many variables. The thesis's 'continuum' examples are largely Russo and Zou's examples relabelled. What remains new is the translation from 'bias of an estimate' to 'excess confirmation', and that translation is the step that needs defending.

closest_work.work: Dwork, Feldman, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold & Roth (2015, Science; NeurIPS 2015 'Generalization in adaptive data analysis and holdout reuse'); Rogers, Roth, Smith & Thakkar (2016, FOCS), 'Max-Information, Differential Privacy, and Post-Selection Hypothesis Testing'
closest_work.relation: Rogers et al. already apply leakage measures to the validity of hypothesis tests chosen after seeing data. They show that p-values remain approximately valid when the selection channel leaks little (max-information, or differential privacy). This is the 'intermediate warrant' claim in testing language. They also use max-information rather than mutual information because MI gives only average-case control. That choice matters for the thesis (see note).

closest_work.work: Fithian, Sun & Taylor (2014), 'Optimal Inference After Model Selection'; Tian & Taylor (2018, Ann. Stat.), 'Selective inference with a randomized response'
closest_work.relation: This is selective inference with randomization ('data carving'). A hypothesis chosen from a noisy version of the data leaves leftover information usable for valid inference, and the amount grows smoothly with the selection noise. This is the 'noisy summary' point on the continuum, already formalized exactly, with no bound needed.

closest_work.work: Hitchcock, C. & Sober, E. (2004, BJPS), 'Prediction Versus Accommodation and the Risk of Overfitting'
closest_work.relation: This is the closest philosophical precedent. It argues that any epistemic advantage of prediction is contingent and stems from the overfitting risk of accommodation, tied to model-selection criteria (AIC). The thesis is in effect an information-theoretic sharpening of Hitchcock and Sober. It should be framed as such, not as overturning a dichotomy.

closest_work.work: Zahar (1973); Worrall (1978, 1989, 2014 'Prediction and accommodation revisited'); Gardner (1982, BJPS), 'Predicting Novel Facts'
closest_work.relation: The claim that timing is neither necessary nor sufficient, and that what matters is whether the data were used in constructing the hypothesis ('use-novelty', 'heuristic novelty'), is standard. It dates to the 1970s and 80s. The pilot-data point is a modest addition.

closest_work.work: Mayo, D. (1996, Error and the Growth of Experimental Knowledge, ch. 8; 2008 with Cox; 2018, Statistical Inference as Severe Testing)
closest_work.relation: Mayo argues that use-novelty is a crude proxy, and that what matters is whether the use of data in constructing H damages the error probabilities (severity) of the test. This is the same structural thesis as yours ('timing/use is a proxy for something else'), with severity in place of mutual information.

closest_work.work: White, R. (2003, Mind), 'The Epistemic Advantage of Prediction over Accommodation'; Lange, M. (2001, Phil Sci), 'The Apparent Superiority of Prediction to Accommodation as a Side Effect'; Barnes, E. C. (2008), The Paradox of Predictivism; Douglas & Magnus (2013, SHPS)
closest_work.relation: These are graded or 'weak' predictivisms on which prediction's advantage is a proxy for some further variable: reliability of the hypothesis-generating process, coincidence-avoidance, or the predictor's credibility. White's 'reliability of the selection mechanism' is close in spirit to treating the selection channel as the relevant variable.

novelty.note: Verdict 'partly'. The mathematics is wholly borrowed, and the continuum with noisy or coarse selection is already explicit in Russo & Zou and in randomized selective inference. The 'timing is a proxy' thesis is decades old (Worrall, Gardner, Mayo, Hitchcock & Sober). I am not aware of a published philosophy paper that explicitly states predictivism as an MI bound on selection leakage, so the bridge itself may be new. I cannot run a literature search here, so check PhilPapers and recent BJPS/Phil Sci/Synthese issues before claiming priority. Whatever novelty there is rests on the bridge, and the bridge has four substantive problems as sketched. (1) Wrong quantity. Russo-Zou bound expected bias of a subgaussian statistic. 'Confirmatory force' of a particular selected H on a particular data set is not an expectation over selection runs. You need an argument that the relevant discount is the average over the selection channel and not conditional on the realized choice. Max-information (Dwork et al.; Rogers et al.) gives high-probability control and is the better-motivated measure for single-case warrant. MI can be small while a rare, highly informative selection event occurs. (2) 'Bounded by' is not 'measured by'. The MI result gives an upper bound, so zero MI implies no bias, but positive MI does not imply a discount of that size, or any discount. The thesis title claims the bound. The argument as sketched supports only sufficiency of zero leakage. (3) The Bayesian objection is not addressed. A Bayesian who conditions on the total evidence, including the fact and mechanism of selection, needs no discount (Howson & Urbach; Kahn, Landsberg & Stockman 1992). 'Excess apparent support' then measures only an agent's failure to condition properly, and MI quantifies how much such a mistake can cost. That is a claim about heuristics, not about confirmation. You must say which. (4) 'Prediction is the special case where information is zero' is false as stated. Theories proposed before the data are typically built on correlated earlier data and background theory, so I(E; choice of H) > 0 for most genuine predictions. Your own pilot-data example concedes this. The framework therefore dissolves the prediction category rather than reconstructing it. That may be the right conclusion, but it should be the stated one.

title: Timing as a Verification Technology
thesis: For an ideal agent with full knowledge of the search process, timing is evidentially irrelevant. For any community whose members cannot verify one another's search histories, it is not. Pre-commitment is the only publicly checkable upper bound on search, so the debate splits into an ideal question (settled against predictivism) and a social question (settled for it).
argument_sketch: Search-based accounts require a description of the search, but searches are largely private, partly unconscious, and cheaply misreported. A temporal record of a proposal before data access is a costly, timestamped commitment that bounds search for anyone who reads it. Drawing on signalling theory, I argue that in equilibrium unverified claims about small searches carry little information. Communities that treat predictions preferentially are therefore rational even if each individual's ideal confirmation is timing-independent. This explains the preregistration movement without endorsing intrinsic predictivism.
why_new: Preregistration is defended in metascience on practical grounds, and the philosophical debate concerns ideal confirmation. Neither side has argued that the two questions get different answers for a precise structural reason, namely the verifiability asymmetry. The thesis also yields concrete conditions, such as auditable search logs, under which the predictive advantage should vanish.

objection.objection: Pre-commitment is not a publicly checkable upper bound on search. The timestamp only bounds search if readers can verify that the proposal was made before the data were accessed, and data access is exactly as private and cheaply misreported as search history. The paper's own signalling argument therefore turns against it. If unverified claims about small searches carry little information in equilibrium, so do unverified claims of 'I hadn't looked yet.' This matters most for observational, archival, pilot, or shared data, where most accommodation worries arise. Even with access verified, a single preregistration does not bound the relevant search. Researchers can file several plans and report one, or search heavily before filing over prior data, pilot results, and colleagues' findings. The pre-filing search is what Lipton's fudging and Hitchcock and Sober's overfitting concerns are about, and the timestamp is silent on it. What actually does the bounding is institutional machinery: registered reports with in-principle acceptance, third-party data escrow, sealed holdout sets, blinded analysis, and mandatory registry disclosure. These are not 'temporal records of a proposal.' Some of them (escrow, holdouts, blinding) bound search without any priority in time. So the uniqueness claim ('the only publicly checkable bound') is false. The bounding claim holds only for data that did not exist at commitment, or under enforcement structures that do the work independently of timing.
objection.rationale: This attacks the load-bearing premise rather than a side claim. The social half of the thesis ('settled for predictivism') rests entirely on pre-commitment playing a unique, verifiable bounding role. If that role belongs to enforcement institutions, two things follow. First, the paper explains why communities rationally reward audited constraints on analysis, not why they reward prediction as such. Second, the residual cases where timing alone suffices (data generated after commitment) collapse into ordinary temporal novelty and gain nothing from the signalling apparatus. The objection is not fatal, because a weaker conclusion survives: under some enforcement regimes, timestamped commitment is a cheap and useful component of a bound. But that weaker thesis does not stand out from existing weak predictivism. Maher (1988), Kahn, Landsberg and Stockman (1992), White (2003), and especially Barnes (2008, The Paradox of Predictivism) already argue that prediction matters to evaluators who lack access to the agent's background beliefs and methods. Hitchcock and Sober (2004) give the overfitting version. The economics literature on pre-analysis plans already models the signalling and its limits (Olken 2015; Coffman and Niederle 2015; Banerjee et al. 2020). Unanswered, the objection leaves the paper with either a false strong thesis or an unoriginal weak one. The author needs to concede scope, recast the unit of analysis as verified constraint rather than time, or show why time-stamping does work that escrow and blinding cannot.

closest_work.work: Peter Lipton, Inference to the Best Explanation (1991; 2nd ed. 2004), ch. 10 on prediction and the 'fudging' explanation
closest_work.relation: Closest anticipation of the core mechanism. Accommodation carries a risk of fudging, and the risk is hard to detect, even by the theorist. Prediction rules fudging out, so a predicted success is better evidence than an accommodated one, even though the evidential link between theory and data does not depend on timing. Your 'searches are private, partly unconscious, cheaply misreported' premise is essentially Lipton's. What you add is the move from the individual to the community, plus a signalling-equilibrium gloss.

closest_work.work: Eric Christian Barnes, The Paradox of Predictivism (CUP 2008); also Barnes, 'Prediction versus accommodation', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
closest_work.relation: Develops 'weak' or 'tempered' predictivism. Prediction matters only as a symptom of something else, such as the predictor's background beliefs or reliability. Barnes explicitly frames the issue around evaluators who lack direct access to the predictor's reasoning, and he distinguishes this case from the case where everything is known. Your ideal-versus-social split is a sharpened version of this structure.

closest_work.work: Christopher Hitchcock & Elliott Sober, 'Prediction versus Accommodation and the Risk of Overfitting', BJPS 55 (2004)
closest_work.relation: Argues that predictive success is evidence that overfitting has not occurred. They concede that if we knew directly how a model was constructed, timing would add nothing. This is your 'ideal question' verdict, reached from model-selection theory rather than from Bayesian idealization.

closest_work.work: James A. Kahn, Steven E. Landsburg & Alan C. Stockman, 'On Novel Confirmation', BJPS 43 (1992); and 'The Positive Economics of Methodology', Journal of Economic Theory 68 (1996)
closest_work.relation: Probably the closest formal precursor to your signalling argument. They treat the researcher's search effort and type as unobservable to the audience and derive a value for prediction from that informational asymmetry. Your 'in equilibrium, unverified claims about small searches carry little information' result should be checked against their models before you claim it as new.

closest_work.work: Patrick Maher, 'Prediction, Accommodation, and the Logic of Discovery', PSA 1988; Roger White, 'The Epistemic Advantage of Prediction over Accommodation', Mind 112 (2003)
closest_work.relation: Both argue that prediction is evidence about the reliability of the method or predictor. White frames this as an inference the evaluator draws under ignorance of the theorist's process. Both are standard weak-predictivist accounts that your view would be classed alongside.

closest_work.work: Heather Douglas & P.D. Magnus, 'State of the Field: Why Novel Prediction Matters', SHPS 44 (2013)
closest_work.relation: Surveys accounts like yours. They argue that the value of novel prediction is partly practical and social (guarding against post hoc fitting and similar risks) rather than purely confirmational. They are close to your 'rational for communities, not intrinsic' conclusion.

closest_work.work: Deborah Mayo, Error and the Growth of Experimental Knowledge (1996), ch. 8; Statistical Inference as Severe Testing (2018)
closest_work.relation: Argues that use-novelty and timing are proxies. What matters is severity, which data-dredging undermines whether or not the search is disclosed. Mayo's work supplies the 'timing is not fundamental' half of your thesis, and it is a standing objection to your claim that pre-commitment is the only relevant check.

closest_work.work: Brian Nosek et al., 'The Preregistration Revolution', PNAS 115 (2018); Mark Rubin, 'Does Preregistration Improve the Credibility of Research Findings?', The Quantitative Methods for Psychology 16 (2020); Szollosi et al., 'Is Preregistration Worthwhile?', Trends in Cognitive Sciences 24 (2020)
closest_work.relation: The methodological debate your thesis claims to explain. Nosek et al. defend preregistration as a way of making the prediction/postdiction distinction publicly visible. Rubin, and Szollosi et al., argue that the work is done by transparency about undisclosed flexibility, not by timing per se. Rubin's argument directly contests your 'only publicly checkable bound' premise.

novelty.note: The overall shape is well established. Timing is not intrinsically evidential, but it is a valuable proxy because the accommodation process is opaque. That is weak or tempered predictivism (Lipton, Maher, Hitchcock & Sober, White, Barnes). Kahn, Landsburg & Stockman already model the unobservable-search asymmetry in economic terms. What may be new: (i) the explicit two-level framing, with the ideal question going against predictivism and the social question going for it; (ii) a signalling-equilibrium argument that unverifiable small-search reports carry little information, without which preferential treatment of predictions would be unjustified; and (iii) applying this to preregistration specifically. These would make a modest but publishable contribution only if the equilibrium result is shown to differ from Kahn et al. Substantive problems a referee will press: (a) 'Only publicly checkable upper bound' is false as stated. Blind analysis, held-out or sequestered data, independent replication, multiverse and specification-curve analyses, and full code-and-log disclosure all bound or expose search publicly. Your thesis needs a weaker comparative claim. (b) Preregistration does not bound search. Multiple or vague preregistrations, undisclosed deviations, and file-drawered preregistered studies are documented problems. So the 'costly signal' is cheaper and noisier than the argument needs, and in Spence-style terms you must show that the cost is differentially harder for high-search agents to bear. (c) 'Settled against predictivism' for the ideal agent is too quick. White and Maher argue that even a coherent Bayesian who lacks information about the predictor's reliability should favour prediction. Your ideal agent is stipulated to have full knowledge of the search, which makes the verdict close to trivial and leaves out the interesting intermediate cases. (d) The individual/community split risks an aggregation gap. If each member, reasoning ideally about what they actually know (which excludes others' searches), already favours prediction, then the 'social' rationality is just individual weak predictivism under realistic ignorance, and the claimed divergence between the two levels disappears.
